nameStory: The Emerald Spreadwing gets its name from the brilliant metallic green sheen that covers its body, making it look like a living jewel when sunlight hits it just right. Like all spreadwings, it holds its wings horizontally away from its body when at rest, rather than folding them back like most damselflies do. This distinctive wing position makes it easy to spot among the cattails and sedges where it likes to hang out.
description: The Emerald Spreadwing is a slender damselfly with a stunning metallic green body that catches the light like polished copper. Unlike most damselflies that fold their wings along their back, this species spreads its clear wings horizontally when perched, giving it an almost airplane-like silhouette. Adults typically measure about 1.5 to 2 inches long with a delicate build and large, prominent eyes. You'll often see them clinging vertically to plant stems near ponds and wetlands, their emerald bodies gleaming in the summer sun.

idTips.label: Wing Position
idTips.description: Wings held horizontally away from the body when at rest, not folded back along the body like most damselflies - this spreadwing posture is unmistakable

idTips.label: Body Color
idTips.description: Brilliant metallic green body with a bronze or copper sheen that shifts in the light - feels smooth and hard to the touch if handled gently

idTips.label: Perching Style
idTips.description: Often perches vertically on plant stems, gripping tightly with spiny legs - tends to stay motionless for long periods

idTips.label: Eye Size
idTips.description: Large, bulging compound eyes that are proportionally bigger than many other damselflies - appear almost jewel-like up close

idTips.label: Wing Clarity
idTips.description: Wings are completely clear and colorless with fine, delicate veining visible when backlit by sun

habitat: Look for Emerald Spreadwings around shallow ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams with plenty of emergent vegetation like cattails, sedges, and rushes. They prefer areas with both open water and dense plant growth, often in partially shaded spots where the water stays cool. You'll find them most commonly in wetlands that don't completely dry out in summer, as they can tolerate harsher conditions than many other damselflies.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, but numbers are still low. Look for recently emerged individuals with soft, pale coloration that haven't yet developed their full metallic sheen.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from July through August when adults are most abundant and actively mating. This is the best time to spot their brilliant emerald coloration and observe their distinctive spreadwing posture.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, often becoming more concentrated around shrinking water sources. Look for egg-laying behavior as females insert eggs into plant stems.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off with the first hard frosts. Eggs overwinter in plant tissues and underwater debris, completely dormant until spring warmth triggers development.

funFact: Emerald Spreadwings are the ultimate damselfly survivors - they can live in water so salty or acidic that it would kill most other dragonflies and damselflies, making them one of the few odonates that can thrive in harsh bog environments and even some polluted waters.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other spreadwings in the Lestes genus, but the Emerald Spreadwing's brilliant metallic green body color sets it apart from the duller browns and bronzes of its relatives. Remember: if it's holding its wings spread and glowing green like a tiny emerald, you've found your spreadwing!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'dryas' (which refers to tree nymphs in Greek mythology), this species actually prefers open wetlands over wooded areas. The scientific name might reflect their habit of perching on woody stems and shrubs around pond edges rather than any particular fondness for forests.
compareHints: Among New England's spreadwings, the Emerald Spreadwing stands out for its brilliant metallic green coloration - most others like the Swamp Spreadwing appear more bronze or brown. The Amber-winged Spreadwing has distinctly tinted wings while the Emerald's remain clear, and the Slender Spreadwing is noticeably more delicate in build. If you see a spreadwing that looks like it's been dipped in green metal polish, you've found the emerald!

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's spreadwings, the Slender Spreadwing is distinguished by its exceptionally thin body profile and pale blue face coloration.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Spotted Spreadwing is one of the easier ones to identify thanks to its distinctive wing spots.
Among New England's nine Lestes species, Swamp Spreadwings are distinguished by their strong preference for heavily vegetated wetlands and their larger, more robust build.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Amber-winged is distinguished by its wing coloration when present, though this can be subtle.
Among New England's spreadwings, the elegant spreadwing is distinguished by its bronze-brown coloration and medium size.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Northern Spreadwing is distinguished by its preference for more permanent water bodies compared to species like the Swamp Spreadwing which favors temporary pools.
Among New England spreadwings, sweetflag spreadwings are distinguished by their preference for heavily vegetated wetlands rather than open water.
